entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4535"/><div sID="gen6567" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4535"/><hi type="bold">7. Yet--</hi>rather, "Truly," or, But affliction does not come from chance, but is the appointment of God for sin; that is, the original birth-sin of man. Eliphaz passes from the particular sin and consequent suffering of Job to the universal sin and suffering of mankind. Troubles spring from man's common sin by as necessary a law of natural consequences as sparks (Hebrew, "sons of coal") fly upward. Troubles are many and fiery, as sparks (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.12">1Pe 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.2">Is 43:2</reference>). Umbreit for "sparks" has "birds of prey;" literally, "sons of lightning," not so well. <div eID="gen6567" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4543"/><div sID="gen6578" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4543"/><hi type="bold">17. happy--</hi>not that the actual suffering is joyous; but the consideration of the righteousness of Him who sends it, and the end for which it is sent, make it a cause for thankfulness, not for complaints, such as Job had uttered (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.11">He 12:11</reference>). Eliphaz implies that the end in this case is to call back Job from the particular sin of which he takes for granted that Job is guilty. Paul seems to allude to this passage in <reference osisRef="Heb.12.5">He 12:5</reference>; so <reference osisRef="Jas.1.12">Jas 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.12">Pr 3:12</reference>. Eliphaz does not give due prominence to this truth, but rather to Job's sin. It is Elihu alone (Job 32:1-37:24) who fully dwells upon the truth, that affliction is mercy and justice in disguise, for the good of the sufferer. <div eID="gen6578" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4545"/><div sID="gen6580" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4545"/><hi type="bold">19. in six ... yea, in seven--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.6.16">Pr 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.3">Am 1:3</reference>). The Hebrew idiom fixes on a certain number (here "six"), in order to call attention as to a thing of importance; then increases the force by adding, with a "yea, nay seven," the next higher number; here "seven," the sacred and perfect number. In all possible troubles; not merely in the precise number "seven." <div eID="gen6580" type="x-p"/>

"Sin" does not agree with the context. The Hebrew word--"to miss" a mark, said of archers (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.16">Jud 20:16</reference>). The Hebrew for "habitation" primarily means "the fold for cattle"; and for "visit," often to "take an account of, to number." "Peace" is the common Eastern salutation; including inward and outward prosperity. <div eID="gen6586" type="x-p"/>
